query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: During elevated-temperature exposure, the degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is primarily governed by oxidation‐induced segregation of reactive elements (especially Ti, Al, and Cr) at grain boundaries. This leads to the formation and subsequent growth of brittle oxide-based precipitates (or intermetallic/sigma-like phases) along the boundaries that drastically impair intergranular cohesion. In reducing environments, the absence or suppression of these oxide films interferes with this degradation pathway but can promote alternative in‐situ phase changes that also weaken the material, providing an explanation for the observed catastrophic failures.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy produced via additive manufacturing with a relatively homogeneous microstructure containing fine, possibly supersaturated precipitates in the as-produced state.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the oxygen partial pressure during high-temperature exposure by running parallel tests under controlled oxidizing (e.g., pure O2 or air) and reducing (e.g., H2 or inert gas with low oxygen content) atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposures in the range of approximately 950–1100 K (where phase transformations and oxidation kinetics are active), for prolonged durations sufficient to allow diffusion‐controlled grain boundary segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary precipitates formed by the oxidation (or related phase transformation) of reactive species (Ti, Al, Cr) that concentrate at the boundaries; these act as weak links by embrittling the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures in an oxidizing atmosphere, accelerated diffusion at the grain boundaries promotes oxidation of the reactive elements. The resulting oxide precipitates (or mixed intermetallic phases similar to sigma phases) coalesce along the boundaries, produce stress concentrations, and reduce cohesion, eventually triggering intergranular cracking and catastrophic mechanical failure. Under reducing conditions, the absence of these oxide films may delay this particular degradation mechanism, but any alternative phase instability from non-equilibrium segregation might still lead to failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-manufactured baseline, samples exposed in oxidizing atmospheres will show significant formation of brittle grain-boundary precipitates (detectable by microscopy and XRD) along with pronounced reductions in intergranular toughness and hardness, eventually leading to early onset of cracks and failure. In contrast, samples in reducing atmospheres will exhibit a lower density of such precipitates and delayed or altered failure modes.
generation.baseline: As-manufactured HEA with an FCC matrix showing homogeneous elemental distribution and limited initial precipitate formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under prolonged high-temperature exposure (950–1100 K) in gas environments that are distinctly oxidizing versus reducing; behavior outside these conditions (e.g., much lower temperatures or extremely rapid thermal transients) may not follow the same mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude and kinetics of grain-boundary oxidation and associated precipitate growth are sensitive to alloy composition nuances and processing histories, so the exact rate of degradation and failure threshold are uncertain. Furthermore, while oxidation appears to be central in governing embrittlement, the role of alternative phase transformations under reducing conditions remains less precisely quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 specimens from identical additive manufacturing batches. Expose one set to an oxidizing environment (e.g., air or controlled O2 at 1000 K) and a second set to a reducing environment (e.g., Ar/H2 atmosphere with very low oxygen) for the same durations. Post-exposure, perform detailed microstructural characterization (SEM, TEM, XRD) focusing on grain boundaries, and mechanical characterization (microhardness, fracture toughness tests) to assess changes in intergranular cohesion.
measurements: Grain boundary precipitate density and morphology (via microscopy)
Phase identification (XRD analysis to detect oxide or sigma-like phases)
Mechanical properties such as hardness and fracture toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidized specimens do not show a statistically significant increase in grain-boundary precipitate formation and corresponding reductions in intergranular mechanical properties (compared to both the baseline and reducing-atmosphere specimens), or if both oxidizing and reducing environments yield similar degradation signatures, the proposed mechanism of oxidation-induced boundary embrittlement will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Meanwhile, the corrosion behavior of the Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 high entropy alloy seems to follow mechanisms observed in conventional alloys, which is controlled by the thermodynamic stability of corrosion products relative to fluorine potential and the level of impurities in the salt. Similar results were observed during the corrosion of CrFeNiCo, CrFeNiCoMn, and CrFeNiCuMn high entropy systems in various aqueous solutions. That being said, it is not sufficient to draw conclusions about the role of the high entropy of mixing and sluggish diffusion in the corrosion behavior of HEAs. More experimental results with various HEAs in different salt media would be needed to better understand the behavior of HEAs in these corrosive environments.

Whereas up to a certain working temperature fine precipitates can play a reinforcing role, starting from a temperature of about 950 K, the σ phase tends to swell and to preferentially place itself on the grain boundaries of the alloy. This in turn can lead to a significant reduction of the mechanical and chemical properties.
